title: The Great Dying and the recovery
summary: About 252 million years ago eruptions in Siberia triggered the worst extinction in Earth's history, wiping out most life in the sea and much of it on land. This story follows the world before the disaster, the killing itself, and the slow recovery that ended with the first dinosaurs.

chapters.title: A Permian reef in Texas
chapters.place: El Capitan, Guadalupe Mountains, Texas, USA
chapters.text: Pangaea, the single supercontinent, stretched from pole to pole, and warm shallow seas lapped its edges. One of them, the Delaware Sea of today's Texas and New Mexico, was ringed by a great reef built mostly by lime-making algae, microbes, sponges and tiny colonial animals called bryozoans, not by corals as today. Around 260 million years ago falling sea level cut the sea off from the ocean, it dried out, and salt and mud buried the reef. Lifted by faults in the last 20 million years, the reef now stands as the cliff of El Capitan, and Carlsbad Caverns are carved into the same rock.

chapters.title: Lava in China, a first crisis
chapters.text: Around 260 million years ago lava flooded what is now south-west China, building the Emeishan Traps, named after Mount Emei. They still cover more than 250,000 square kilometres, though far smaller than the Siberian eruptions to come. At about the same time a crisis struck: big single-celled fusulinids, corals and tropical reefs collapsed in the sea, and in South Africa's Karoo the giant plant-eating and meat-eating dinocephalians vanished. How big this end-Capitanian extinction was is disputed: some count it among the great mass extinctions, others see a smaller or more local event.

chapters.title: Sabre-teeth and tusks in the Karoo
chapters.place: Karoo Basin near Graaff-Reinet, South Africa
chapters.text: In the last part of the Permian, rivers wound across the Karoo in the far south of Pangaea, lined by forests of Glossopteris, a seed-bearing tree with tongue-shaped leaves that grew across the southern continents. The commonest large animals were dicynodonts, beaked plant-eaters with two tusks, from burrowing Diictodon to much bigger kinds. They were hunted by gorgonopsians, sabre-toothed relatives of mammals up to about 3.5 metres long, such as Rubidgea and later Inostrancevia. Layer after layer of Karoo mud preserves this world right up to its end.

sites.name: Karoo Basin, Beaufort Group rocks
sites.note: River muds up to 6 kilometres thick hold one of the richest records of Permian land animals.

chapters.title: Siberia bursts into flame
chapters.text: About 300,000 years before the great extinction, lava began to pour out across Siberia. Roughly two-thirds of all the Siberian Traps erupted in about 300,000 years, and about 7 million square kilometres of basalt survive today. Just as important, sheets of magma pushed sideways underground through a basin full of coal, limestone and salt. Baking these rocks released enormous amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases, including chlorine compounds that can harm the ozone layer.

sites.name: Putorana Plateau
sites.note: Stacked lava flows form the step-like cliffs of this remote plateau.

chapters.title: The Great Dying at Meishan
chapters.text: In a quarry at Meishan in eastern China, limestone full of fossils gives way within a few beds to rock where most of them are gone. Ash layers dated with great precision show that the main extinction began about 251.94 million years ago and was over within about 60,000 years, a blink in geological time. Just before it, the chemistry of carbon in the sea lurched, a sign of huge amounts of carbon entering the air. Meishan is the world's reference point for the start of the Triassic, marked by the first appearance of the tiny conodont Hindeodus parvus.

sites.name: Meishan section, Permian-Triassic boundary stratotype
sites.note: Five dated ash beds bracket the extinction and the boundary.

images.caption: The share of sea animal genera dying out in each slice of time over 540 million years; the tallest spike, over 50 percent, is the end of the Permian.
images.note: A graph, not a picture of the place; it counts genera, not species.

images.caption: A spiny productid brachiopod from Permian Texas; nearly all productid species vanished in the Great Dying.
images.note: From the Glass Mountains of Texas, about 270 million years old, not from Meishan.

chapters.evidenceNote: Uranium-lead dates on zircon crystals from five volcanic ash beds at Meishan pin the extinction to between 251.94 and 251.88 million years ago.

sources.title: Burgess, Bowring & Shen 2014, PNAS: High-precision timeline for Earth's most severe extinction

chapters.title: Forests fall and the coal stops
chapters.place: Frazer Beach, Sydney Basin, New South Wales, Australia
chapters.text: On the coast near Sydney the last Permian coal seam is capped by grey lake mud: the Glossopteris forests that made the coal died out here a few hundred thousand years before the extinction in the sea. Worldwide about 81 percent of marine species and about 70 percent of land vertebrate species were lost. It was also the greatest known extinction of insects, and perhaps the only one that cut their diversity deeply. No coal at all is known from the earliest Triassic anywhere: peat-forming swamp forests took millions of years to return.

sites.name: Frazer Beach, Munmorah State Conservation Area
sites.note: The last Permian coal is overlain by lake muds laid down just after the Glossopteris forests died.

images.caption: The Permian-Triassic boundary at Frazer Beach: the black band at the bottom is the last Permian coal, with grey and sandy Triassic layers above.
images.note: Portrait format.

images.caption: Tongue-shaped Glossopteris leaves from the late Permian of Australia, from the trees whose forests collapsed at the end of the Permian.
images.note: Shown at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, Canada.

chapters.evidenceNote: Fossil pollen and spores in rock layers dated by zircon crystals show the Glossopteris flora vanishing from the Sydney Basin before about 252.1 to 252.3 million years ago.

chapters.title: Too hot, too acid, too breathless
chapters.place: Nanpanjiang Basin, Guizhou and Guangxi, China
chapters.text: Oxygen in the tiny teeth of conodonts from south China works like a thermometer, and it suggests tropical seas warmed to around 40 degrees Celsius, with peaks that came and went for millions of years. Warmer water holds less oxygen while animals need more, and models suggest this alone explains over half of the losses in the sea. Shell chemistry also points to a sharp drop in ocean pH as the extinction began. How much each of these mattered, and whether the acid was global, is still disputed; ozone loss, acid rain and mercury poisoning may have added to the toll on land.

sites.name: Nanpanjiang Basin sections, south China
sites.note: About 15,000 conodonts from rocks here were used to track Early Triassic sea temperatures.

sites.name: Meishan, Zhejiang
sites.note: Sea surface temperature here rose about 10 degrees Celsius during the extinction.

chapters.title: Lystrosaurus inherits the Earth
chapters.text: On land one survivor stood out: Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized dicynodont with a beak and two tusks. For a while about 95 percent of the backboned land animals in South Africa's earliest Triassic rocks were Lystrosaurus, something no other land animal has ever matched. Its bones turn up in South Africa, India, China and Russia, and in 1969 to 1970 Edwin Colbert's team found them at Coalsack Bluff in Antarctica, strong evidence that these lands were once joined. Growth marks in Antarctic tusks suggest it could slow down through the dark polar winters, a lifestyle that may have helped it survive.

chapters.title: A slow and patchy recovery
chapters.place: Paris Canyon, Bear Lake County, Idaho, USA
chapters.text: For millions of years many seas were dominated by a few hardy survivors, such as the thin-shelled clam Claraia, and recovery kept stalling as new heat spikes and a further extinction about 249 million years ago struck. Yet some places bounced back early. Near Guiyang in south China a full food web of fish, shrimp and ammonoids was living about 250.8 million years ago, only a million years after the extinction, though some researchers doubt it lasted. At Paris in Idaho, rocks about 249 million years old hold sponges, ammonoids, fish and early squid relatives. Small reefs built by animals came back after a few million years, but corals of the modern kind appeared only in the Middle Triassic, about ten million years after the Great Dying.

sites.name: Guiyang biota, Guizhou, China

images.caption: A slab crowded with the thin shells of Claraia, a clam that flourished in the emptied seas just after the extinction, from the Dolomites of Italy.

chapters.title: Reptiles go back to sea
chapters.text: Within a few million years reptiles had taken to the emptied seas. At Chaohu in eastern China, rocks about 248 million years old hold Chaohusaurus, a metre-long early ichthyosaur, including a mother with babies, one apparently being born head first. Beside it lived Cartorhynchus, about 40 centimetres long with flipper-like limbs and a short snout, a close cousin of the ichthyosaurs that may still have crawled onto land. Tail bones from Spitsbergen about 250 million years old show ichthyosaurs already at sea, and their finders suggest the group began even before the extinction.

chapters.title: Ruling reptiles and dinosaur cousins
chapters.text: As the land recovered, the archosaurs, the 'ruling reptiles' that include crocodiles and dinosaurs, spread fast; sail-backed Ctenosauriscus lived in Germany about 248 million years ago. The Manda Beds of Tanzania show how early the dinosaur line split off. They hold Teleocrater, one of the oldest known reptiles on the bird and dinosaur side of the family, Asilisaurus, a slender silesaurid one to three metres long and close cousin of the dinosaurs, and Nyasasaurus, perhaps the earliest dinosaur of all. These rocks are usually dated to about 245 million years ago, but some scientists argue they are millions of years younger.

chapters.title: Rain falls and dinosaurs spread
chapters.text: About 234 million years ago huge eruptions in what is now western North America warmed the planet, and for one to two million years the dry Triassic world turned rainy. Marine life suffered again, but on land the old plant-eaters such as most dicynodonts and rhynchosaurs declined. In the Dolomites, footprints show no dinosaurs before the rains, about 40 percent dinosaur tracks during them, and over 90 percent soon after. The oldest well-dated dinosaur skeletons, in Brazil and at Ischigualasto in Argentina, come from just this time: 20 million years after the Great Dying, the age of dinosaurs was beginning.

sites.name: Dolomites footprint sites
sites.note: Dated trackways show dinosaurs appearing exactly when the rains began.

sites.name: Santa Maria Formation, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
sites.note: Saturnalia and Staurikosaurus are dated to about 233 million years ago.

sites.name: Ischigualasto, San Juan, Argentina
sites.note: Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus lived here soon after the rainy episode.

images.caption: Piz Ciavazes in the Dolomites: the soft sloping layer between the cliffs records the Carnian rainy episode, when muddy rock replaced reef limestone.

chapters.evidenceNote: Climate signals in rock layers and dated footprints and skeletons tie the dinosaurs' spread to the rains, but some studies argue the rainy episode was not the main cause.
